rationale: Abnormal clinical EEG mostly shows up as changes in spectral shape: diffuse or focal slowing, a slowed or missing posterior dominant rhythm, and excess fast activity from medication. Five broad bands blur these patterns. I'll replace them with a 1 Hz-resolution log relative spectrum (1–45 Hz, per channel), estimated with median-averaged Welch so that transient artifacts in this unclean data have less effect. Because there are far more features now, the logistic regression penalty strength is picked by inner grouped CV on the training fold.

Five fixed bands hide two things that mark an abnormal clinical EEG: posterior alpha slowing (a peak shift inside the 8–13 Hz band) and changes in the shape of the spectrum. This replaces them with the log relative spectrum in 1-Hz bins from 1–45 Hz per channel. The PSD uses median-averaged Welch, which resists artifacts, and the logistic-regression regularization strength is tuned by inner grouped CV, because the feature count rises from 95 to 836.

Abnormal clinical EEGs differ from normal ones in overall amplitude and slowing, and in finer spectral detail (for example a slowed or missing alpha peak, or excess beta from medication). The current 5 relative bands throw most of that away. This change adds log absolute power in 1-Hz bins from 1 to 45 Hz per channel, computed with median-averaged Welch so it is robust to artifacts, on top of the existing relative bands. The logistic regression's C is now chosen by inner grouped CV, because the feature set grows to about 930 dimensions.

The main sign of an abnormal clinical EEG is slowing: the posterior dominant rhythm drops below about 8 Hz and there is too much delta/theta. Five wide bands blur this, because a 9 Hz rhythm and an 8 Hz rhythm both land in "alpha". I'm replacing the five bands with finer log relative power: 1-Hz bins from 1 to 20 Hz, 2-Hz bins from 20 to 30 Hz, and one 30–45 Hz bin. The Welch window goes from 2 s to 4 s so the 1-Hz bins are better resolved. The classifier stays the same, so any gain comes from the features.

Abnormal clinical EEG mostly shows up as focal or diffuse slowing and changes in overall amplitude. Those effects are non-linear and local, so I switch from the linear model to LightGBM gradient boosting and give it a richer spectral set: log absolute power plus log relative power in 9 finer bands, each channel's total 1-45 Hz power, and channel-averaged band powers, all from a median-averaged Welch PSD that resists artifacts.

Clinical EEG abnormality often shows up as narrow spectral changes, such as the alpha peak shifting to lower frequencies or focal delta/theta activity. Five broad bands blur these out, so I replace them with a log relative spectrum in 1 Hz bins (1–45 Hz) per channel. The spectrum uses median-averaged Welch, which keeps it robust to amplitude scale and to the unrejected artifacts in clinical recordings. Because this gives about 19×44 features, the logistic regression's strength C is now tuned with inner grouped CV on the training fold only.

I'm replacing the 5 coarse relative bands with a finer, more robust spectrum. Each channel gets a log-relative spectrum in 2-Hz bins (1–45 Hz) from a median-averaged Welch PSD, which resists the artifacts left in this unprocessed clinical data, plus the channel's log total power. That keeps the detail of clinical abnormalities, such as focal slowing and changes in the dominant rhythm and beta, that 5 coarse bands blur together. Because the feature count grows from 95 to about 440, the logistic regression's strength (C) is now chosen by grouped inner CV on the training fold only.

Five wide bands blur the spectral changes that mark an abnormal clinical EEG, such as focal or diffuse slowing, a slower alpha peak and beta excess, and Welch mean-averaging lets artifact bursts dominate. I'm swapping in a full-resolution log relative spectrum (1-Hz bins from 1–45 Hz, median-averaged Welch so artifacts have less pull) plus each channel's log total power, keeping the L2 logistic regression. Because the feature count rises from 95 to about 870, I pick C with grouped inner CV on the training fold.

Abnormal clinical EEGs mostly show up as slowing, e.g. a slower posterior alpha rhythm or extra theta/delta in certain channels. Five broad bands blur these shifts, so I'm adding per-channel log relative power in 1-Hz bins (1–45 Hz) alongside the existing band features. Because the feature count grows from 95 to about 950, the logistic-regression strength C is now tuned with grouped inner CV on the training fold.

I'm replacing the five coarse relative band powers with each channel's full log spectrum: 1 Hz bins from 1 to 45 Hz, normalized by total power, plus that total power on a log scale. Clinically abnormal EEG shows up as patterns the five bands blur: focal or diffuse slowing at specific delta/theta frequencies, a slowed or missing alpha peak, and beta excess from medication. The logistic regression's regularization strength C is now chosen by patient-grouped inner CV on the training fold only.

I'm replacing the 5 coarse relative bands with log absolute power in 9 finer bands plus log total power, using a median-averaged Welch PSD. Abnormal clinical EEG shows up as focal or diffuse slowing in sub-bands (1–2 vs 2–4 Hz, 6–8 Hz, and low vs high alpha) and as changes in overall amplitude, which relative power throws away. The logistic regression can still rebuild relative power from these features (log band minus log total), and the median average keeps short artifact bursts in these unrejected clinical recordings from dominating the spectrum.

Five fixed bands smear the main signs of an abnormal clinical EEG: a slower alpha peak, focal or diffuse delta/theta slowing, and beta from medication. This change uses log relative power in fine bins instead: 1-Hz bins from 1–30 Hz and 3-Hz bins from 30–45 Hz, for every channel. Because the feature count grows (about 650), the logistic-regression strength C is now picked by patient-grouped inner CV on the training fold. Normalizing each channel by its total power keeps the features independent of amplitude scale.

Five coarse relative bands throw away the spectral shape that marks abnormal clinical EEG: diffuse or focal slowing, a slowed or missing posterior alpha peak, and overall amplitude changes. I'm replacing them with a log absolute-power spectrum per channel, in 1-Hz bins from 1–20 Hz and wider bins above that, taken from a robust median-Welch PSD. Because the feature set is now much larger, the L2 penalty of the logistic regression is picked by grouped inner CV on the training fold. I haven't run this yet, so I don't have a Dev score for it.

I'm replacing the five coarse relative bands with a finer log spectrum: 1-Hz bins from 1 to 45 Hz on every channel, normalized by total power, plus each channel's log total power. The spectrum is median-averaged across Welch windows so that bursts of artifact in a clinical recording carry less weight. The fine bins can pick up the main abnormal signs: diffuse or focal slowing, an alpha peak shifted lower, and changes in beta. The logistic regression C is now chosen by inner grouped CV on the training fold, since the feature count is much higher.

I'm replacing the five coarse relative bands with a fine-grained log spectrum per channel (1-Hz bins from 1 to 45 Hz, each normalised by that channel's total power) plus each channel's log total power. Abnormal clinical EEG shows up as narrow spectral changes: focal or diffuse delta/theta slowing, a slower or missing alpha peak, and extra beta from medication. Wide bands blur these together. Because the feature count goes from about 95 to about 850, I now choose the logistic-regression penalty C by grouped inner CV on the training fold only.

Abnormal clinical EEG mostly shows up as focal or diffuse slowing, a slower or lost posterior rhythm, and changes in beta. Five broad bands blur these, so I replace them with a fine relative log-spectrum (1-Hz bins, 1–45 Hz, per channel) plus log total power per channel. The PSD uses median-averaged Welch, which resists artifacts, and the logistic-regression C is tuned by inner grouped CV on the training fold.

I'm adding filter-bank covariance matrices (5 bands, 19×19) per recording. They are mapped into Riemannian tangent space with a reference point fitted on the training fold only, and sit alongside the existing relative band powers. The idea is that abnormal clinical EEG shows up in spatial patterns of absolute power and cross-channel coupling (focal or lateralised slowing, diffuse delta, disorganised background), and per-channel relative power can't see those. The regularisation strength C is now picked by inner CV grouped by patient instead of being fixed at 0.1. I haven't run this; the harness will give the score.

Five broad relative bands discard the fine spectral shape that marks abnormal clinical EEG, such as focal or diffuse slowing, a shifted or missing alpha peak, beta excess from medication, and overall amplitude changes. This round I'm replacing them with a robust log absolute spectrum in 2-Hz bins (median Welch, so short artifact bursts don't dominate) per channel. The L2 logistic regression's C is now tuned by inner grouped CV, because the feature count goes from 95 to 418.

Five broad relative bands hide the details that mark a clinically abnormal EEG: focal or diffuse slowing inside delta/theta, a slowed or missing alpha peak, and beta excess from medication. Absolute amplitude, which relative power throws away, matters too. This version uses the log-relative spectrum in 1-Hz bins (1–45 Hz) plus log total power for each channel. It fits a logistic regression whose regularization strength C is chosen by inner CV grouped by patient, since the much larger feature set needs C retuned. I have not run it, so I don't yet know whether it beats the current Dev score of 0.8547.

I'm replacing the five coarse relative bands with a finer relative log-spectrum: 1 Hz bins from 1 to 45 Hz, computed with a median-averaged Welch PSD so short artifact bursts have less effect. I'm also adding each channel's share of total power, which describes how power is spread across the scalp without depending on overall amplitude. Clinical abnormality (focal or diffuse slowing, loss of the posterior dominant rhythm, asymmetries) shows up at finer frequency and spatial detail than five bands capture. The logistic-regression strength is now tuned by grouped inner CV on AUROC.
